messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai was a 74-year-old software engineer who had spent most of her career writing code for a defense contractor, working from home in recent years. She was married, with two grown children, but the memory that shaped her life came from when her youngest son was five years old. He had developed a sudden, severe bacterial infection that spiraled into septic shock within hours. She remembered the frantic drive to the hospital—her husband at the wheel, her son limp and feverish in her lap—and then the long, sterile hallways, the antiseptic smell that seemed to cling to her clothes even after they had been discharged weeks later. He had survived, but the experience had carved something permanent into her.

In the years that followed, Mai found herself avoiding certain things without fully understanding why. The smell of rubbing alcohol or bleach made her stomach clench, and she would step out of a room if someone opened a bottle of cleaning solution. Car sounds—the rumble of an engine, the screech of tires, even the quiet hum of a vehicle idling—could send ice down her spine, and she had stopped driving altogether, letting her husband take her everywhere. But it was silence that frightened her most. She had come to believe that when the world went quiet, something terrible was about to break through. At night, she could not let herself fall asleep easily; she would lie rigid in bed, ears straining for any sound, as if staying awake were a shield. Her husband had learned to leave a fan running in their bedroom, the constant whir a small comfort against the threat of complete stillness.

At work, she had adapted. She kept a small white-noise machine near her desk, and she wore headphones while coding, listening to podcasts or music. But the hypervigilance had a cost: she was always scanning, always waiting for a signal of danger. The world, she was certain, was a dangerous place, and she had no power to stop bad things from happening. Worse, she carried a deep, private shame. When she thought back to those days in the hospital—the terror, the helplessness—she felt a hot wave of guilt. The event had happened because of the way she acted, she believed. She should have noticed the fever sooner, should have pushed the pediatrician harder, should have demanded a different course of treatment. Her son had lived, but her own failure felt indelible.

Sometimes, without any clear image or memory, she would be overcome by the full emotional force of that time—a sudden plunge into terror so raw she would have to sit down, gasping, unable to say why. These episodes had become more frequent in the past year. She had retired from full-time work but continued consulting, and the quieter hours at home gave silence more room to creep in. Her husband had noticed she was sleeping even less, that she flinched at the mail truck or a distant siren. Finally, he had asked her to talk to someone. She agreed, partly because she was exhausted, and partly because she had begun to wonder if she was losing her mind.

What brought Mai to the clinic was not the old trauma itself, but a recent, almost minor event. A neighbor had been airing out their house with the windows open, and the faint smell of hospital-grade disinfectant had drifted into her kitchen. She had dropped a glass, shattered it, and found herself on the floor, shaking, unable to breathe. That night, she had lain awake for hours, certain that something awful was about to happen, though she could not name what it was. She was afraid of being afraid, and she was hoping, quietly, that someone could tell her how to stop the world from feeling so dangerous—because at 74, she was tired of guarding against a threat that never came.
